title: AI Uptake Remains Slow in Japan
paragraphs: Artificial intelligence is spreading rapidly around the world, but according to several recent surveys, Japanese companies are adopting the technology more slowly than many of their international competitors.

In a survey carried out for the Reuters news agency by Nikkei Research between late July and early August 2026, 219 Japanese companies were asked about their use of AI. Only 16% said they had introduced AI across their entire company as an essential tool. Around 60% said they used AI only in some parts of their business or in other limited ways, while 18% had not yet decided whether to introduce it. Another 6% said they were not considering using AI at all. In other words, 84% of the companies were making limited or no use of the technology.

Some companies explained the challenges they faced. For example, a manager at a wholesale company said that although AI had been introduced across the company, it was only being used for tasks such as creating documents. Meanwhile, an official at a real estate company admitted that the company did not know how to make use of AI.

Other research supports these findings. A government report released earlier in 2026 found that 86.4% of Japanese companies used generative AI for at least one task. However, this was lower than in China, at 98.1%, Germany, at 91.6%, and the United States, at 90.9%. Some experts have also pointed out that using AI for at least one task is a very broad definition.

In addition, Japanese companies appear less satisfied with the results. In a survey by PwC Japan of about 3,000 managers in six countries, only 9% of Japanese respondents said that AI had exceeded their expectations, the lowest figure of all the countries surveyed. In comparison, 38% of respondents in the United States said AI had performed well above their expectations. In Japan, AI was mainly used for tasks such as writing reports and emails.

Experts warn that slow adoption could make it harder for Japan to achieve its goals of improving productivity. Nevertheless, the Reuters survey found that no companies expected to spend less on AI over the next one to two years, and 25% expected their AI budgets to grow by at least 10% a year.
